items.text: We got in on a Friday night, but wait was long. The kitchen was clearly in over its head. If you do go in you'll get a decent meal, but you'll also have to put up with that slow service. You can get the same result at a bunch of other places around town, and the good stuff here is just too easy to get at the bad. I'd rather eat somewhere that gets both right. Baan Noi will run you around $22 a head, but for what you get it's fair. Order the pad see ew. It has good texture and the noodles actually taste like something. Don't bother with the green curry. They load it down with sugar and it ends up cloying. That's not the only thing that dragged the meal down.

Wanted to see O, but it was on hiatus so we went to La Rêve instead. We were staying at Encore and it was just a walk to the theater. We got seats in the third row. La Rêve is always compared to O, so I thought it was a pretty good substitute. It's not O, but it's a good substitute. I think there's a story but I didn't understand it, but that wasn't a big deal to me. The first part of the show, before the main event, there's a comic lizard-guy swimming in the pool and standing still, like a statue. Then he sneaks up and spits water on the people in the front rows. The main event is the pool, the platforms go up and down. People swim and dive, and they make it look like they're walking on water. Then they dive into the pool from about 25 feet. If you want a really good Vegas show that isn't Cirque du Soleil, which is super expensive, La Rêve is a good substitute. We enjoyed it.

A rain gauge is simple. You look at the circular opening at the top and measure the rain that's falling. The water gets funneled into a small measuring tube. It is calibrated to measure millimeters or inches. That's the depth of rain. If you were to put it on the ground, and let all the rain hit the ground, this would be the depth of water that you get if it didn't run off or get absorbed.

The opening is much larger than the tube. That means that it gets concentrated into a smaller column. This makes it easier to measure small amounts of rain. The scale on the tube is calibrated to correct for the difference in area. The scale is calibrated so that the depth is accurate. The two main problems with rain gauges are that they're not well-placed, or they're not read often enough. For example, if it's near a tree, it will be sheltered from the rain, or you'll get splashing off the tree. Or if it's near a building or fence, you'll get too much rain. If you don't read it quickly, you'll have evaporation.

I have a book that appears in my bakery every Thursday. Wedged between flour bins and cooling racks. I have looked for the book for eleven Thursdays now, checked the locks, asked the day staff. Nothing. The book has never been found to have been placed there at a specific time. It just appears, sometime between two and four in the morning.

The book is called *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. Cracked spine, faded library stamp, due date long passed. Tonight it was heavier than usual. When I opened it, a little square of receipt paper fell out. It reads: I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on, and I think: somebody is awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.

I read it twice. The ovens ticked behind me. The first trays of rye were waiting under cloths. I turned the receipt over, found a stub of pencil behind my ear, and wrote on the back: don't stop. Then I tucked it back in the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window, and left the light on.

It was two-forty in the morning. In the basement, the sour smell of the rye fermenting really overpowered the bleach and the floor. Arthur wiped his hands on his jeans. He went and rummaged behind the wicker bannetons, on the wire rack down low, the library had a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo, it was taped up. Fourth Thursday. Same as the others, the spine lined up with the steel edge. He pulled it out. Stuck to the cover was a square of blue prescription pad paper, and it said in ballpoint, the ink had gone through: the baker in chapter five reminds me of you, thank you for keeping the lights on. Arthur traced with his thumb the deep indentation the pen had left. The only sound was the compressor shuddering. Out of the back of the book fell a due date card, yellowed, red ink, stamped three days overdue. He went to the prep table, took a warm cinnamon roll, it had glaze spots, wrapped it in parchment paper, put it in his coat pocket with the book.

Four stars, keeping it. The space bar rattles. When I hit it with my thumb it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key sticks sometimes and I type eexample. It happens once an afternoon when I type fast and don't look at the keys.

I paid $38, I kept it anyway because of the switches. I asked the seller what switches they were. A week later the seller said brown tactile switches. I had already pulled off the keycap and found out for myself. It has a bump and a soft landing at the bottom of the stroke. Old membrane keyboard felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, 2-3 hours at a time, wrists don't ache by the end. That mattered more than the rattle.

I could send it back, pay for postage, box it up and be without keyboard while I waited. So it stays on my desk. Now I tap the spacebar closer to the middle.

It was about two years ago. We called Rockmount Ranch Wear to order two shirts for my dad. Never heard of them. The sales rep got the address wrong. Wrote down 7 as a 1. We were supposed to get them to 5407. So, that's what happened. The people at 5401 brought it back to UPS. And then it disappeared. No one ever saw it again. We didn't know for weeks. Then we ordered two more shirts, just to see what happens. Rockmount said no refund on the first two shirts. The owner came in on this. He said the shipment was to the wrong address. He said no refund until the shirts were returned. He said we're partly responsible for not being friendly enough to the folks at 5401, which is four doors away. We disputed the original charge with the credit card company. And we got a credit.

I want to warn people about Turkish Airlines. I had a domestic flight from Harbin to Beijing, then my connection to Istanbul. Since the first flight was delayed, I missed my connecting flight. The staff at the counter refused to take responsibility, and I ended up sleeping in the terminal. They told me the next day that economy was overbooked and said I'd have to wait days or pay for business class. I had to be in Istanbul, so I paid. I'm still fuming and honestly in disbelief about Turkish.

The book drop was a milk crate by the back door. Every Thursday, around two o'clock, Imre would find something that wasn't milk. First week, A Field Guide to Mushrooms of the Northeast, Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week, same book. Third week, same. He'd stopped reshelving it in his head. It lived on the flour bench now, between the scale and the rye starter, cover gone soft with thumbprints. Tonight he slid the crate out with his hip, oven mitts on. The book was there again, heavier than usual. A yellow square of paper stuck out around page 112. He peeled off the mitts. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard to the right. "Your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? -T." Imre looked at the page. The morel sat there, wrinkled and brown. He pulled the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note over, and wrote "No. Never used one." Then, after a moment, he added "Come at five, there's bread." He pressed it back into the book.

So, Marisol was working the night shift, around 3:17. The cooler kicked on, the proofing cabinet was just breathing, all that low hum. She got the first loaves in the oven. And next to the back door, there's a wicker basket. The same old paperback was there again: The Borrowers. For six Thursdays straight, somebody had just left the book there instead of taking it to the library two blocks away. No name on the checkout card, just a barcode and a coffee ring. She found a note folded up between pages 84 and 85, wiped her hands on her apron and read: I can't get to the library before it closes, please keep it another week, I like knowing it's warm. So she looked at the basket, then at the cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack, picked the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, put the note back in the book, and left them both by the door. Then at 4:50, she pulled the loaves, knocked them out of the pans, and slid the next tray in.

I got this second-hand mechanical keyboard for $38. I didn't have big expectations. I didn't want missing keycaps, sticky grime, or gravel switches. It does what it should. Came clean enough I didn't need to clean it. The keys feel really nice and weighty. It's really nice for me as I type long emails, I don't really get a sore finger, which I get with other cheaper new keyboards. So I do like it, but it's not perfect. Space bar does rattle, if you hit it off-center it will rattle a little bit, so it's not the cleanest feel, but it's not too bad. One of the keys sometimes repeats, I'll be typing and looking up and there's a letter in the middle of a sentence. So it's not perfect. And the communication with the seller was not great. I asked what switches are in it, took a week to answer me. And I'd already pulled the keycap off and checked for myself. So it is flawed, but usable. So I thought about returning it, but it's just too much effort for $38.

Honestly, Vegas isn’t really my thing. I’ve been going there pretty much my whole life, or at least the under 21 version of it, so I’ve seen a ton of shows. And yes, Le Reve at Wynn, I finally caught. And I’m very mixed on it. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good things. It’s a circular stage, which is really cool because you’re looking down, so it’s good no matter what seat you’re in. That’s rare in Vegas. Some of the individual acts were really good, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are serious athletes. But it felt very much like Cirque du Soleil. Not a rip-off, but if you’ve seen Cirque du Soleil, you’ve seen the same stuff done better. And the clarity thing. What’s the story? I don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? But it’s just a bunch of pretty pictures. The show didn’t tell you what it was trying to say. There’s so much happening at once, too many people, too many elements, too many things you’re supposed to be wowed by. More restrained would have been better. It felt like typical Vegas, more is better, so they put everything in.

I got it for 99 because I’m staying at Wynn, instead of 125. Would I see it again? Probably not. And I wouldn’t pay for it again. I’m not blown away by it, and I don’t think anyone else is. It’s just a good show, and I’m sure some people enjoy it. So, if you’re going to Vegas and you haven’t seen Le Reve, you should go. But don’t expect to be overwhelmed.

Got a second hand mechanical keyboard, bought it for $38 so wasn’t expecting perfection, and that is pretty much what I got. It arrived reasonably clean, and it worked right away, which was a relief. The typing feel is actually better than I expected. I write long emails for work, and the keys are comfortable enough that my hands don’t feel tired after an hour or two. The space bar rattles noticeably if I hit it near the edges. Makes it sound cheaper than it feels. Also, one key occasionally repeats. Annoying when you type fast and have to go back and delete the extra letter. Doesn’t happen constantly, but enough to mention. I did ask the seller about the switches, and she answered my question, but it took a full week to get a reply. By then I’d figured it out. I considered returning it, but for $38, didn’t seem worth the trouble of shipping it back. Overall, I kept it. It’s comfortable and usable, just not flawless.

It's a fourth Thursday in a row. The same library book, this time leaning against the flour bin by the back door. Every week she drops it in the return box on her way home, and by Thursday, someone's got it checked out and brought it back. The first time she saw it, it was 3:40, while the second batch of rye was proofing. It's *A Field Guide to Night Birds* from Eastgate Branch, and it's got a fresh due-date slip on it. This time it had a folded index card inside. She opened it and found it on the barn owls page, where someone had penciled a check mark beside the line for the call. It says, "You leave the vent fan on, the alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog at half past three because she can't anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking this out again. - R." She read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, the fan was rattling steam across the wet dumpster lid. She turned the card over and with her grease pencil, the one she uses for marking trays, she wrote, "Rye's out at 4:15." Then she took a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, set it on the outside step, laid the book on top, and propped the back door open about an inch.

The food wasn't really something I could judge. The whole experience was a mess. We got there at 7:20 on Sunday because we needed time before our show at 10. The hotel buffet's digital waitlist is ridiculous. We were told to come back to pay at 8:23, but we waited till 8:40, and then the staff told us we would probably not be seated till 9:15. They didn't offer any solutions. The manager could have let us know about the long wait times, or at least past the payment time, if they had a solution. That would have saved us hours. Basic hospitality failed. If I could give it 0 stars I would.

So you got 2,600 more meals out the door this quarter than spring, and that mostly came from the three new drivers. They can hit the outlying routes the old crew couldn't. You've got 12,400 meals banked against that. Best showing in a while. The thing holding you back is the walk in freezer. It's been out long enough to eat into storage and it will take the full 7,500 to fix. You can keep the current pace going once fixed. If the repair money doesn't come in the next month, you'll have to turn some walk in traffic away. The drivers are in place. The demand is clearly there. You just don't have the storage to keep up with it. Your spring numbers show what the group's capable of. So what's left is getting that equipment in working order.

Bought this keyboard used for 38 dollars. Knew that price doesn't buy perfection. It didn't. Spacebar rattles, not every press, but often enough that I notice it in the silence before I start writing. One key repeats too, will type a word and find a double letter in the middle. I reread everything before hitting send. Saved me from a few other mistakes, I think. Would rather the keyboard had not forced it. Asked seller what switches before buying, got answer a week later, too late. I'd already ordered it and started learning the feel. Why I keep it: comfort. I write long emails, sort of past the point where you stop paying attention to your hands. This one doesn't tire them. Keys have weight that I like. After an hour I'm still typing same pace. Thought about shipping back, kept it. Rattle is less annoying than packing a box.
